questions.q: What is a CI/CD pipeline, concretely, per this lesson?
options: A single tool that replaces the need for version control
A manual checklist a developer follows before emailing a change to an admin
An ordered sequence of automated stages, where each stage only runs if the previous one succeeded, triggered by an event in version control
Any Salesforce org that has at least one sandbox
questions.explain: A pipeline is an ordered, gated sequence of automated stages triggered by a version-control event -- the tool running it (like GitHub Actions) is a separate design choice from this shape.

questions.q: Why should a fast static analysis check typically run before a slow Apex test suite in a pipeline?
options: There's no reason to wait 20 minutes for a full test run to discover a problem a 20-second linter check would have caught instantly -- cheap, fast checks should run before slow, expensive ones
Static analysis and Apex tests can never run in the same pipeline
Apex tests must always run first by Salesforce platform rule
Static analysis replaces the need for Apex tests entirely
questions.explain: This 'shift left' ordering principle puts the cheapest, fastest checks first so a pipeline fails fast instead of burning time on slow checks before discovering a trivial problem.

questions.q: In the typical branch-to-environment mapping example in this lesson, what happens when a pull request merges into an 'integration' branch?
options: Nothing happens automatically
It triggers a real deploy to a shared integration sandbox
It immediately deploys to production with no further steps
It deletes the feature branch's static analysis results
questions.explain: In the example mapping, merging into the shared integration branch is what triggers an actual deploy to the shared integration sandbox, as opposed to the validation-only checks a feature branch gets.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about the relationship between a team's sandbox count and its Git branching model?
options: They are completely unrelated and can be changed independently with no consequence
Branching models are only relevant to open-source projects, not Salesforce teams
Sandbox count has no bearing on pipeline design at all
They are usually designed together -- changing one without revisiting the other tends to produce a pipeline that doesn't match how the team actually works
questions.explain: The number of environments and the branching model are coupled design decisions -- a mismatch between them is a common source of pipelines that don't fit a team's real workflow.

questions.q: What is a 'quality gate' in the pipeline stage order this lesson describes?
options: A pass/fail decision point that can block everything downstream if coverage, tests, or static analysis didn't meet the bar
The first stage, which always checks out the repository
A step that only runs after production deployment is complete
A manual email sent to the release manager with no automated check
questions.explain: A quality gate is the decision point in the pipeline that can halt later stages (like promotion to the next environment) if earlier automated checks didn't pass.
